etymology.root: English rowan, recorded from 1804 and detached from an earlier rowan-tree, rountree, attested in northern English and Scots from the 1540s; probably from a North Germanic source related to Old Norse reynir, ultimately from Germanic *raud-inan 'to redden', for the berries.
etymology.note: The tree's Old English name was cwic-bēam, which survives as quickbeam. By the nineteenth century that name had been reinterpreted through the dialect form wick, producing wicken-tree, wich-tree and wiggan-tree — so the tree ends up sounding as though it were named for the witches it was cut against.

text.what: Two rowan twigs laid across each other and bound at the crossing with red thread or wool, a few inches across. A variant is a loop rather than a cross: a single withy bent round and tied. Both are cut green, and both are meant to be renewed.
text.story:
The rowan's reputation is older than the charm's paperwork. British folklorists of the Victorian era reported the belief in the tree's power to turn away witches: Edwin Lees wrote it up for the Wyre Forest in 1856, James Frazer reported it from Scotland in 1890 — where the tree was often planted by a gate or a front door — and Charles Godfrey Leland reported English traditions of the same in 1891, citing the Denham Tracts, collected between 1846 and 1859. Frazer singled out the flying rowan, a rowan seeded by bird droppings into the fork of an oak or a maple and growing as an epiphyte, as especially potent against witches and as a counter-charm against sorcery.

What the twigs were for is agricultural before it is anything else. In Scottish folklore boughs of rowan were taken into cattle byres in May to protect the livestock, rowan trees were planted in pastures for the same reason, and twigs were used to drive cattle out to grass for the first time in spring to secure their health and fertility. In English folklore the wood was worked into the shafts of farm implements to keep animals and produce out of reach of witches' spells, and rowan was chosen for the post or mantel over a fireplace. Thomas Keightley recorded that mortals could safely watch the fairy rades — the mounted processions the fairies were said to hold at the onset of summer — by putting a rowan branch over their doors.

The objects survive because a clergyman posted them to Oxford. On 28 February 1893 the Rev. Canon John Christopher Atkinson, of Danby Parsonage, Grosmont, in the North Riding of Yorkshire, gave the Pitt Rivers Museum three rowan loops, accessioned as 1893.18.1–3, the smallest 70 mm across; Atkinson had published on the practice in 1891. The museum's account records that from Scotland to Cornwall crosses of the same wood were bound with red thread and carried in pockets or sewn into the linings of coats, and that in Strathspey a loop of rowan was made at May Day and flocks of sheep and lambs were driven through it morning and evening.

*Tradition holds —* the charm goes with a couplet, usually given in Scots as "Rowan tree and red thread, gar the witches tyne their speed" — gar is to compel, tyne is to lose. This record has not read that rhyme in any of the sources it cites, and prints it here as a thing people say rather than as a documented text.
text.how: Cut green, from a living tree, at a named time — the Pitt Rivers account gives St Helen's Day for collecting, and May Day and Lammas for the rites the loops belong to. Two twigs are crossed and lashed at the join with red thread or wool; a loop is bent from one withy and tied. The finished charm goes over a door or a byre lintel, into a pocket, or into a coat lining. *Tradition holds —* it is cut fresh each year, the old one discarded, which is why so few reach museums.
text.today: Made and sold by British craftworkers and by shops trading in folk charms, and made at home by people who have read about it. *Inference —* the continuous farming practice the Victorian folklorists recorded is not what is happening now; what is happening now is a revival working from those same published accounts, and this record separates the two rather than running them together.

dating.period: Victorian folklore record to the present
dating.label: recorded from the 1840s; still made
dating.note: Dated from the earliest collections this record has read: the Denham Tracts, gathered 1846–1859; Edwin Lees on the Wyre Forest, 1856; Frazer on Scotland, 1890; Atkinson's Yorkshire loops, given to the Pitt Rivers Museum in 1893. The practice is certainly older than its first collector and this record does not guess how much older.

object.made_by: anyone in the household; no restriction is recorded
object.note: The Pitt Rivers Museum records three loops from Atkinson, the smallest 70 mm across. That is a measurement of one object in one accession, not a typical dimension, so it is not entered as length_mm.
